summary.text: A Fibonacci-type lower bound on the common power of two dividing both recurrence components shows that, for every fixed $k$, $2^k\mid a(n)$ once $n\ge 2k+6$. Finite state analyses modulo $3$ and $7$ show that $a(n)=0$ would force respectively $n\equiv2$ and $n\equiv1\pmod 3$, so every term is nonzero and its $k$-th prime factor is therefore eventually always $2$ (period $1$).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n,b_n)\) be the integer sequences defined by
\[
(a_0,b_0)=(1,1),\qquad (a_1,b_1)=(2,1),
\]
and, for every \(n\geq 0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+2}&=a_{n+1}b_n+a_nb_{n+1},\\
b_{n+2}&=a_{n+1}b_n-a_nb_{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus A382590 is the sequence \(a_n\).

For a nonzero integer \(x\), its prime factors are understood to be the prime factors of \(|x|\), written in nondecreasing order and counted with multiplicity. The stated definition of the \(k\)-th prime factor returns \(1\) if there are fewer than \(k\) factors, but we will show that this exceptional clause never applies once \(n\) is sufficiently large.

We prove the stronger conclusion that, for each \(k>1\), the \(k\)-th prime factor of \(a_n\) is identically \(2\) for all
\[
n\geq 2k+6.
\]
It will then be eventually periodic with period \(1\).

## 1. A growing power of two dividing both components

Define a sequence \(M_n\) of nonnegative integers by
\[
M_0=M_1=M_2=M_3=0,\qquad M_4=M_5=1,
\]
and
\[
M_n=M_{n-1}+M_{n-2}\qquad(n\geq 6).
\]
We first prove
\[
2^{M_n}\mid a_n\quad\text{and}\quad 2^{M_n}\mid b_n
\tag{1}
\]
for every \(n\), where divisibility here is in \(\mathbb Z\).

The first recurrence values are
\[
(a_0,b_0)=(1,1),\quad (a_1,b_1)=(2,1),\quad
(a_2,b_2)=(3,1),\quad (a_3,b_3)=(5,1),
\]
\[
(a_4,b_4)=(8,2),\qquad (a_5,b_5)=(18,-2).
\]
Consequently (1) holds for \(0\leq n\leq 5\): for the first four indices the required power is \(1\), and for indices \(4,5\) both components are even.

Now suppose \(n\geq6\) and (1) is known at \(n-1\) and \(n-2\). Write
\[
a_{n-1}=2^{M_{n-1}}A,
\quad b_{n-1}=2^{M_{n-1}}B,
\quad a_{n-2}=2^{M_{n-2}}C,
\quad b_{n-2}=2^{M_{n-2}}D.
\]
The defining recurrence gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_n&=2^{M_{n-1}+M_{n-2}}(AD+CB),\\
b_n&=2^{M_{n-1}+M_{n-2}}(AD-CB).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(M_n=M_{n-1}+M_{n-2}\), both expressions are divisible by \(2^{M_n}\). Induction proves (1).

We next need a simple lower bound on \(M_n\):
\[
2M_{r+6}\geq r+1\qquad(r\geq0).
\tag{2}
\]
For \(r=0\), this says \(2M_6=4\geq1\), and for \(r=1\), it says \(2M_7=6\geq2\). For the induction step, write \(r=m+2\). From the two preceding induction hypotheses,
\[
2M_{m+7}\geq m+2,
\qquad
2M_{m+6}\geq m+1.
\]
Using \(M_{m+8}=M_{m+7}+M_{m+6}\), we obtain
\[
2M_{m+8}\geq 2m+3\geq m+3,
\]
which is exactly (2) for \(r=m+2\). Thus (2) holds for all \(r\).

It follows in particular that
\[
n\geq2k+6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k\leq M_n.
\tag{3}
\]
Indeed, put \(r=n-6\) in (2). Then
\[
2M_n\geq n-5\geq2k+1,
\]
which certainly implies \(M_n\geq k\).

Combining (1) and (3), for every \(n\geq2k+6\) we have
\[
2^k\mid a_n.
\tag{4}
\]
The same statement is true for \(|a_n|\), because if \(a_n=2^kc\), then \(|a_n|=2^k|c|\).

To use (4) in a statement about prime factors, we must also know that \(a_n\) is never zero. This matters because the prime-factor list of zero is treated exceptionally.

## 2. No term \(a_n\) is zero

We establish nonvanishing by two finite modular-state computations, modulo \(3\) and modulo \(7\).

For a modulus \(q\), consider the state
\[
S_q(n)=\bigl(n\bmod3,\ a_n\bmod q,\ b_n\bmod q,\ a_{n+1}\bmod q,\ b_{n+1}\bmod q\bigr).
\]
If a state is written \((r,x,y,X,Y)\), the recurrence says that its successor is
\[
T_q(r,x,y,X,Y)
 =\bigl((r+1)\bmod3,\ X,Y,\ Xy+xY,\ Xy-xY\bigr),
\tag{5}
\]
with the last four entries reduced modulo \(q\).

### The computation modulo \(3\)

Starting from
\[
S_3(0)=(0,1,1,2,1),
\]
direct use of (5) shows that every state belongs to the following five-element set:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
 &r&x&y&X&Y\\ \hline
1&0&1&1&2&1\\
2&1&2&1&0&1\\
3&2&0&1&2&1\\
4&0&2&1&2&2\\
5&1&2&2&0&1
\end{array}
\]
More explicitly, the transitions are
\[
1\longmapsto2\longmapsto3\longmapsto4\longmapsto5\longmapsto3.
\]
Thus the set contains the initial state and is closed under the transition, so induction on \(n\) proves that it contains \(S_3(n)\) for every \(n\).

Inspection of the table shows that whenever the current \(a\)-coordinate \(x\) is zero modulo \(3\), the first coordinate is \(2\). Hence
\[
3\mid a_n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n\equiv2\pmod3.
\tag{6}
\]

### The computation modulo \(7\)

Likewise, starting from \(S_7(0)=(0,1,1,2,1)\), the states encountered are the following 31 states, all entries after the first being residues modulo \(7\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
1&0&1&1&2&1\\
2&1&2&1&3&1\\
3&2&3&1&5&1\\
4&0&5&1&1&2\\
5&1&1&2&4&5\\
6&2&4&5&6&3\\
7&0&6&3&0&4\\
8&1&0&4&3&4\\
9&2&3&4&5&5\\
10&0&5&5&0&5\\
11&1&0&5&4&3\\
12&2&4&3&6&6\\
13&0&6&6&0&1\\
14&1&0&1&6&1\\
15&2&6&1&6&6\\
16&0&6&6&0&5\\
17&1&0&5&2&5\\
18&2&2&5&3&3\\
19&0&3&3&0&2\\
20&1&0&2&6&1\\
21&2&6&1&5&5\\
22&0&5&5&0&3\\
23&1&0&3&1&6\\
24&2&1&6&3&3\\
25&0&3&3&0&1\\
26&1&0&1&3&4\\
27&2&3&4&3&3\\
28&0&3&3&0&3\\
29&1&0&3&2&5\\
30&2&2&5&6&6\\
31&0&6&6&0&4
\end{array}
\]
Here each row again has the form \((r,x,y,X,Y)\). Substitution into (5) gives the transitions
\[
1\to2\to3\to\cdots\to31\to8.
\]
Thus these states form a forward-closed set containing the initial state, and consequently every \(S_7(n)\) occurs in the table.

In every row whose current \(a\)-coordinate \(x\) is zero, the first coordinate \(r\) is \(1\). We conclude that
\[
7\mid a_n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n\equiv1\pmod3.
\tag{7}
\]

If \(a_n=0\), then it is zero both modulo \(3\) and modulo \(7\). Statement (6) would give \(n\equiv2\pmod3\), while (7) would give \(n\equiv1\pmod3\), an impossibility. Therefore
\[
a_n\neq0\qquad\text{for every }n\geq0.
\tag{8}
\]

## 3. From divisibility to the \(k\)-th prime factor

We use the following elementary fact. If \(x\neq0\), \(k\geq1\), and
\[
2^k\mid |x|,
\]
then the \(k\)-th prime factor of \(x\), counted with multiplicity and ordered nondecreasingly, is \(2\).

To justify this carefully, let the prime factorization list of \(|x|\) be
\[
p_1\leq p_2\leq\cdots\leq p_s.
\]
Because \(x\neq0\), the usual prime factorization applies. The number of occurrences of \(2\) in this list is the exponent \(v_2(|x|)\). The divisibility \(2^k\mid|x|\) says exactly that \(v_2(|x|)\geq k\). Thus the list has length at least \(k\). Every prime is at least \(2\), and the list is nondecreasing; since it contains at least \(k\) copies of \(2\), its first \(k\) entries must all be \(2\). In particular, its \(k\)-th entry is \(2\). This also shows directly why the exceptional value \(1\) for a too-short factor list does not arise.

For completeness, the assertion that the first \(k\) entries are \(2\) can also be seen by induction through the sorted list. If its first entry were greater than \(2\), then every entry would be greater than \(2\), contradicting the existence of any occurrence of \(2\). Hence its first entry is \(2\); remove it and repeat, decreasing both the desired number of entries and the known count of copies of \(2\) by one.

Now fix \(k>1\), so in particular \(k\geq1\), and let
\[
N_0=2k+6.
\]
For every \(n\geq N_0\), (1) and (3) imply \(2^k\mid a_n\), hence \(2^k\mid|a_n|\). By (8), \(a_n\neq0\). The preceding prime-factor argument therefore gives
\[
\operatorname{kpf}_k(a_n)=2
\qquad(n\geq N_0),
\tag{9}
\]
where \(\operatorname{kpf}_k\) denotes the \(k\)-th prime factor counted with multiplicity.

The same applies to \(n+1\), since \(n+1\geq N_0\). Consequently, for every \(n\geq N_0\),
\[
\operatorname{kpf}_k(a_{n+1})=2=
\operatorname{kpf}_k(a_n).
\]
Thus the sequence of \(k\)-th prime factors is eventually periodic with the positive period
\[
p=1,
\]
and one may take the explicit starting index \(N_0=2k+6\). In fact, it is eventually constant, equal to \(2\), which proves the conjecture.
